claims.text: High-temperature exposure stabilizes multi-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles through temperature-induced surface segregation.
Oxidation-resistant elements preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Elements with low atomic diffusivity preferentially migrate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-segregated elements form a protective passivating shell.
The passivating shell impedes nanoparticle-core coarsening.
The passivating shell suppresses phase segregation.
The passivating shell suppresses further oxidation.
Rapid high-temperature synthesis can produce stable multi-element nanoparticles.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles have a uniform elemental distribution.
Elevated temperature increases atomic mobility and produces preferential diffusion of particular elements to the surface.
The resulting surface layer minimizes subsequent diffusion from the nanoparticle core.
Surface passivation preserves the overall equiatomic distribution during service.
Surface passivation preserves nanoparticle structural integrity under harsh operating conditions.
Increasing the content of oxidation-resistant elements will reduce coarsening relative to an untuned equiatomic baseline.
Increasing the content of oxidation-resistant elements will reduce phase segregation relative to an untuned equiatomic baseline.
Passivation-engineered nanoparticles will retain higher catalytic performance than untuned equiatomic nanoparticles after high-temperature exposure.
Passivation-engineered nanoparticles will retain higher thermoelectric performance than untuned equiatomic nanoparticles after high-temperature exposure.
The mechanism requires appreciable differences in oxidation potential and diffusivity among constituent elements.
The proposed stabilization mechanism remains applicable at temperatures up to approximately 1923 K.
A layered oxide with compositionally distinct Ni-rich, Cr-rich, and Fe/Mn/Co-rich regions can develop during oxidation of equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies low-diffusivity elements as the species preferentially transported to the surface, while the mechanism requires sufficient mobility and preferential diffusion to create the shell. No additional thermodynamic driving force is specified to reconcile low diffusivity with preferential migration.
The boundary requires atmospheres where oxidation is significant but lists inert environments as an example; genuinely inert conditions do not ordinarily provide significant oxidation.

Surface segregation is required to create the proposed stabilizing shell, but the outcome is described broadly as reduced phase segregation. The fields do not clearly distinguish beneficial surface segregation from detrimental internal phase separation.
